title: Verbal clash: absolute-faith subject vs living-faith subject
source_text: XXIX. Porro, ut liquet ex dictis, nonnulli Scholae Reformatae Doctores Theologis Scholae Romanae concedunt, fidem in solo intellectu esse, tanquam in proprio subjecto; licet voluntatem quoque moveat & afficiat: sed Reformati plerique utramque facultatem, tam voluntatem, quam mentem subjectum esse fidei contendunt: quod communiter negant Doctores Scholae Romanae. Verum ex iis quoque quae supra fuerunt exposita, patet hic etiam esse contentionem de verbis. Nam quum negant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae fidem esse in voluntate, tanquam in proprio subjecto, fidem, ut jam dictum est, absolute considerant, & secundum illa quae ipsi conveniunt, sive viva, sive mortua sit; quo respectu nullus inter Reformatos affirmabit voluntatem esse fidei subjectum. Quum vero dicunt Doctores Reformati fidem non esse in solo intellectu, sed etiam in voluntate, loquuntur de fide viva & per charitatem operante, prout fidei mortuae & historicae opponitur: Quo respectu Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae non inviti fatentur non solum intellectum, sed voluntatem etiam esse fidei subjectum, quandoquidem ipsis ultro concedentibus, fides sic considerata includit fiduciam & dilectionem ipsam, quae sunt voluntatis actus.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover, as is clear from what has been said, some Reformed Doctors concede to Roman-school theologians that faith is in intellect alone as in its proper subject, though it also moves and affects the will; but most Reformed contend that both faculties, will as well as mind, are faith's subject — which Roman Doctors commonly deny. Yet from what was set out above it is clear that here too there is a contention about words. For when Roman Doctors deny faith is in the will as in a proper subject, they consider faith, as already said, absolutely and according to what belongs to it whether living or dead; in which respect no Reformed will affirm the will is faith's subject. But when Reformed Doctors say faith is not in intellect alone but also in the will, they speak of living faith working through charity as opposed to dead and historic faith: in which respect Roman Doctors not unwillingly confess that not only intellect but also will is faith's subject, since on their own concession faith so considered includes trust and love themselves, which are acts of the will.
pass_b_english: Some Reformed concede intellect-alone as proper subject; most claim both faculties — Rome usually denies.
Much is verbal: Rome means absolute faith (dead or living); Reformed mean living faith, which Rome also seats partly in will via trust and love.

choices.why: Seat of absolute vs living faith.
